problem.title: Design a High-Concurrency LRU & W-TinyLFU Cache
problem.prompt: Design an in-process thread-safe cache for a 64-core API server holding 10M entries (~8 GB, ~800 B/entry) at 1,200,000 `get()`/sec (95% reads, 5% writes) and < 50 us p99 latency. A single-lock `HashMap + DoublyLinkedList` collapses to 140K ops/sec because `get()` mutates the list. Add scan resistance and bounded TTL.

spark.summary: A classic `HashMap + DoublyLinkedList` LRU serializes every read behind a global write lock, collapsing 64-core throughput from 1.2M ops/sec to 140K ops/sec.
spark.keyTakeaway: Eliminate read-path lock contention via 128-way lock striping or Caffeine-style read ring buffers (or SIEVE 1-bit `visited` flags), and pair with W-TinyLFU (1% window + 4-bit Count-Min Sketch) for scan resistance.
spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** Every textbook teaches `HashMap + DoublyLinkedList` for `O(1)` LRU.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts 1% Admission Window -> 4-bit Count-Min Sketch -> Segmented Main (128 Striped Shards -> Read Ring Buffer -> W-TinyLFU (CMS) -> Timing Wheel TTL); Lock-Free Read Buffer Drain & W-TinyLFU Admission Filter (64 Reader Cores -> Striped Read Buffer -> 4-bit CMS Filter -> Main SLRU (99%)).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** A `ReentrantReadWriteLock` still requires an exclusive write lock on `get()` to mutate the LRU list. Scale to `1.2M+ ops/sec` within `8 GB` (`~880 MB` metadata + `7.12 GB` payload): **Zero-Contention Read Path**: Partition into `128` shards (`78,125` entries and `9,375` ops/s per.

**Failure Modes & Application:** Caffeine (Java) and Ristretto/Otter (Go) implement this exact architecture: **L1 In-Process Caches**: Sits in front of Redis/DB in high-QPS API servers to serve `95%` hot reads in `< 50 us`.

learningJourney.title: Why classic LRU fails on 64-core servers
learningJourney.explanation: Every textbook teaches `HashMap + DoublyLinkedList` for `O(1)` LRU. On a 64-core server handling `1,200,000 get()/sec` (`95%` reads), `get()` is *not* read-only: it must unlink the node and move it to the MRU head—forcing a global write lock that caps throughput at `~140,000 ops/sec` (`>85%` CPU spent spinning).

learningJourney.title: Mutex convoying, one-hit scan pollution, and expired-key leaks
learningJourney.explanation:
Three bottlenecks destroy in-process cache performance:

1. **Global Write-Lock Contention**: 64 threads serialize on one mutex (`140k` vs `1.2M` ops/sec).
2. **One-Hit Scan Pollution**: A batch job scanning `10M` cold keys flushes the entire hot working set out of a pure LRU.
3. **Lazy-TTL Memory Leak**: Keys that expire without being read again occupy the `8 GB` budget unless swept.

sectionDiagram.summary: Striped read ring buffers remove read-path locks while W-TinyLFU protects hot entries from sequential scans.

learningJourney.title: Naive `RWLock` and un-aged frequency counters
learningJourney.explanation: A `ReentrantReadWriteLock` still requires an exclusive write lock on `get()` to mutate the LRU list. Meanwhile, a naive LFU without periodic counter halving lets historically hot keys permanently block newly hot keys.
learningJourney.purpose: Scope boundary: identify where this pattern fits best and where simpler or async alternatives win.

learningJourney.title: Enterprise solution: Lock Striping / SIEVE + W-TinyLFU + Timing Wheel
learningJourney.explanation:
Scale to `1.2M+ ops/sec` within `8 GB` (`~880 MB` metadata + `7.12 GB` payload):

- **Zero-Contention Read Path**: Partition into `128` shards (`78,125` entries and `9,375` ops/s per shard) + a Caffeine-style striped **read ring buffer** (drains promotions asynchronously under `tryLock`) or **SIEVE** (`if (!node.visited) node.visited = true;` avoids even dirtying the cache line on hot reads!).
- **Scan Resistance (W-TinyLFU)**: Admit new keys into a `1%` Window LRU; on eviction, a **4-bit Count-Min Sketch** (periodically halved) admits the candidate to Main SLRU only if its frequency beats the Main victim.
- **Active TTL**: Hierarchical timing wheel sweeps expired entries in `O(1)`.

sectionDiagram.title: Lock-Free Read Buffer Drain & W-TinyLFU Admission Filter
sectionDiagram.summary: Readers never wait on list locks; a single tryLock drain updates LRU order and filters one-hit scans via CMS.

learningJourney.title: Where high-concurrency W-TinyLFU caches are used
learningJourney.explanation:
Caffeine (Java) and Ristretto/Otter (Go) implement this exact architecture:

- **L1 In-Process Caches**: Sits in front of Redis/DB in high-QPS API servers to serve `95%` hot reads in `< 50 us`.
- **Database & Storage Block Caches**: RocksDB/CockroachDB Pebble use segmented/clock-pro caches to resist large range-scan pollution.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why does Caffeine use a lossy read ring buffer and W-TinyLFU instead of a global-lock LRU?

options.text: The lossy ring buffer batches LRU promotions off the hot read path without blocking readers, while W-TinyLFU's Count-Min Sketch prevents one-hit scans from evicting hot keys
options.feedback: Correct: decoupling list mutation from `get()` removes mutex contention, and W-TinyLFU adds scan resistance.

options.text: Because `ConcurrentHashMap.get()` cannot store keys larger than 64 bytes
options.feedback: `ConcurrentHashMap` has no 64-byte key limit; the bottleneck in classic LRU is mutating the doubly linked list on every read.

options.text: W-TinyLFU eliminates the need for TTL expiration on cached entries
options.feedback: W-TinyLFU handles eviction policy; TTL expiration still requires a timing wheel or periodic sweep.
